title: What To Do If You Get Lost
html:
Getting lost is a moment, not a disaster. What you do in the next ten minutes decides which one it becomes.

Most lost-hiker stories end with a tired person walking out or being found within hours. The ones that don't usually share one feature: the person kept moving. This guide is about not being that story.

  2. The Moment You Realise — the first ten minutes, and the two instincts that mislead
  3. Retrace or Stay — the one real decision, with a clean test for making it
  4. Being Findable — visible, audible, warm, trackable
  5. If Night Comes First — an unplanned night out, survivably
  6. The Pocket Card — the whole method on one page, to print and fold

Built around one page

Questions

Is this guide for beginners? Yes. It is written in plain words for beginner and intermediate hikers on winter day hikes. It is not mountaineering or avalanche training; it covers avalanche awareness and points you to official sources such as avalanche.org and Avalanche Canada.

What should I wear for a winter hike? Layers you can add and remove: a base layer that moves sweat away, a warm mid layer and a windproof, waterproof shell, and no cotton. The guide includes a layering checklist by temperature in °F and °C.

Why do my headlamp and phone die faster in the cold? Cold slows batteries, so they run down sooner. Start with a full charge, keep them in an inside pocket close to your body, and carry a spare light. The guide has a section on batteries and phones in the cold.

Do I need microspikes? It depends on the trail. The guide explains when boots are enough and when microspikes or snowshoes help, and when to turn back. Check current trail conditions with the park or local rangers before you go.

Is anything shipped? No. It is an instant PDF download, and the download button arrives in your order confirmation email right after checkout.

title: Trail Ready: 8-Week Beginner Hiking Training Plan (Printable)

Have a bigger hike coming up, like a park trip, a first 10-miler or a summit? This printable plan gets you ready in eight weeks without a gym. You only need good shoes, a daypack, some stairs or a hill, and a chair.

What is inside (28 pages)

  • Who the plan is for, what you need, and a quick self-check before you start
  • How it works: five short sessions a week (walks, hikes and strength days), with easier and harder options
  • Warm-up and cool-down routine
  • Strength moves for hikers: step-ups, squats to a chair, lunges, calf raises, glute bridge and plank, each with an easier and a harder version
  • Weeks 1 to 8, one page each: daily sessions, pack weight build-up in lb and kg, distances in miles and km, and a tip of the week
  • The week 8 dress rehearsal hike
  • Going downhill kindly on your knees, food and water on training hikes, and sore vs hurt: when to rest and when to get checked
  • Four weekly training logs, a progress tracker, a pre-trip checklist and a trip-day plan to leave with someone
  • Sources and further reading

Good to know

  • Instant PDF download, no physical item is shipped. Download buttons arrive in your order confirmation email right after checkout
  • US Letter and A4, color and printer-friendly versions included
  • Made for beginner to intermediate hikers
  • General fitness information, not medical advice. If you have health concerns, talk to your doctor before starting a new exercise plan
  • For personal use

Questions

Do I need a gym? No. You need good shoes, a daypack, some stairs or a hill, and a chair. Strength days use simple moves like step-ups, squats to a chair, lunges and calf raises.

I am a beginner. Will it be too hard? Every session and strength move has an easier and a harder version, so you can start where you are. If you have health concerns, talk to your doctor before starting a new exercise plan.

How is a week set up? Five short sessions a week: walks, hikes and strength days, with pack weight and distance building up slowly. Week 8 ends with a dress rehearsal hike.

Miles or kilometers? Both. Distances are in miles and km, and pack weight in lb and kg.

title: Grand Canyon South Rim — Trip Planning Guide
html:
A 30-page printable trip planner for first-time visitors to the Grand Canyon South Rim: when to go, what to book and when, sample 1, 2 and 3-day plans, 6 rim walks and 4 short canyon hikes with honest turnaround points, and the heat and water rules that keep you safe. $9.99, instant PDF download in US Letter and A4.

Planning a first trip to the Grand Canyon? This printable guide puts the whole South Rim trip on paper, so you arrive knowing where to stay, which shuttle to take, which walks fit your group and how far to go below the rim, instead of juggling a dozen open browser tabs.

What is inside (30 pages)

  • The park at a glance: South Rim vs North Rim, Hermit Road, Desert View Drive and the free shuttle routes
  • When to go, season by season, with rim and canyon temperatures in °F and °C, and how to beat the crowds
  • Booking timeline for lodges, campgrounds and the Phantom Ranch lottery, plus the October 2026 entrance fees and passes (including the non-resident fee that applies to Canadian visitors)
  • Airports, gateway towns (Tusayan, Williams, Flagstaff) and the two entrances
  • Sample plans for 1, 2 and 3 days on the South Rim
  • 6 rim walks for every fitness level: Mather Point to Yavapai Point, the Trail of Time, Powell Point to Mohave Point, the Greenway to Hermits Rest, Shoshone Point and Desert View
  • 4 short canyon hikes: Ooh Aah Point and Cedar Ridge on the South Kaibab, and the 1.5 Mile and 3 Mile Resthouses on the Bright Angel. Distance in mi and km, climb in ft and m, from nps.gov, with where to turn around
  • 'Down is optional, up is mandatory': why the climb back out takes longer, and why rim to river and back in one day is not a plan
  • Heat, water and salty snacks, winter ice on the rim trails, altitude, storms and safety at the edge
  • A 'no signal' page, a packing checklist, two day-plan pages, a trip budget sheet and a trip log
  • Official sources, questions to ask a ranger, and a page on visiting with kids and the Junior Ranger program

Good to know

  • Instant PDF download, no physical item is shipped. Download buttons arrive in your order confirmation email right after checkout
  • US Letter and A4, color and printer-friendly versions included
  • Works offline once printed or saved, which matters in a park with limited phone signal
  • Checked against nps.gov in October 2026, including the fall 2026 flood closures. Rules, fees, water stations and trail closures change, so always check current park alerts before you go

Can a beginner hike into the canyon? Yes, if you keep it short and start early. The 4 canyon hikes in the guide each have a clear turnaround point, and every distance and climb comes from nps.gov. The climb back up is the hard part, so the guide explains how to plan for it.

title: First Backpacking Trip — Beginner's Guide & Planner (Printable)
html:
A 32-page printable guide and planner for day hikers ready to spend their first night on the trail: how to pick an easy first route, the gear that matters (and what to borrow or rent instead of buying), sleeping warm, water, simple trail meals, food storage, camp setup and Leave No Trace, plus fill-in planners for the trip, the food and the pack weight. $8.99, instant PDF download in US Letter and A4.

If you are comfortable on 5-8 mile (8-13 km) day hikes, a first overnight is the natural next step. This guide walks you through it in plain words, then gives you the pages to plan it on, so your first night out is easy, safe and fun instead of cold and overpacked.

What is inside (32 pages)

  • A self-check: are you ready for a first overnight?
  • How to pick an easy first route: short distance, water nearby, established campsites and a way out, where to find them (state parks, national forests, national parks) and permits
  • A first-trip timeline: 6 weeks out, 2 weeks out and the night before
  • The big three (pack, shelter, sleep system) explained for a first trip, with what to borrow or rent before you buy
  • Sleeping warm: sleeping bag and pad ratings in plain words, and layers for the night
  • Clothing for the trail and for camp
  • Water: how much to carry, finding sources and treating every source
  • Simple no-cook and boil-only trail meals, and how much food to pack
  • Storing food and smelly things: bear canisters, hangs and lockers, and following the local rule
  • Setting up camp, Leave No Trace for overnights, camp kitchen and stove safety
  • Weather, dark and when to go home early, plus leaving a trip plan and what to do if things go wrong
  • Fill-in pages: a 2-page gear checklist with a lb / kg weight column, pack weight worksheet, how to pack your pack, meal planner, trail food shopping list, trip planner, a trip plan to leave at home, a night-before checklist, an after-trip review and two trip logs
  • Official sources (NPS, US Forest Service, Leave No Trace, state parks) and a backpacking glossary

Good to know

  • 32 pages, US Letter and A4, color and printer-friendly versions included
  • Instant PDF download, no physical item is shipped. Download buttons arrive in your order confirmation email right after checkout
  • Units in both imperial and metric
  • Made for beginners. Day hikes are covered by our Beginner's Hiking Guide; this guide is the next step, with no overlap
  • Rules for permits, fires and food storage differ by park and forest, so always check the official pages or ask a ranger before you go

Is it for complete beginners? It is for people who already enjoy day hikes and want to try a first night out. If you are new to hiking, start with our Beginner's Hiking Guide.

Hiking with your dog is one of the best parts of having one. This guide helps you get the two of you trail-ready step by step, know the rules before you arrive, and pack the right things for both of you.

What is inside (20 pages)

  • Start with your vet: age, breed and health come first
  • Is my dog trail-ready? A self-check for recall, leash manners and fitness
  • Build up slowly: a 4-week start plan in miles and km, and signs your dog needs a rest
  • Where dogs can hike: national parks vs national forests vs state parks, leash rules, the BARK Ranger program, and checking each park's pets page
  • Trail manners: leash, yielding, other dogs, horses and people who are nervous around dogs
  • Water and food on the trail, heat and cold (hot ground, paws, signs of overheating and when to stop)
  • Paw checks and the after-hike tick check for dogs and people
  • Wildlife, streams, lakes and crossings, and why to carry clean water for your dog
  • Poop and Leave No Trace with a dog
  • Fill-in pages: dog first aid kit checklist, dog hiking pack list, your own pack list, a dog ID and emergency card, a trail plan for the two of you and a 2-page dog hike log

Good to know

  • 20 pages, US Letter and A4, color and printer-friendly versions included
  • Instant PDF download, no physical item is shipped. Download buttons arrive in your order confirmation email right after checkout
  • Units in both imperial and metric, for hikers in the US and Canada
  • Not a substitute for your vet. Ask your vet before starting longer hikes, and keep your vet's and the nearest emergency clinic's numbers with you
